title: Supreme Court Says Voter Roll Deletion Does Not Strip Indian Citizenship
excerpt: The court issued notices to the Election Commission and the West Bengal government after millions removed during electoral roll revision were denied welfare benefits.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Supreme Court confirms electoral roll removal doesn't equate to loss of citizenship.
  • 91 lakh voters removed in West Bengal; 34 lakh appeals pending.
  • Deleted voters denied welfare benefits despite unresolved citizenship status.
  • Court scheduled next hearing for August 25; individuals can seek High Court relief.
  • Municipal elections in West Bengal set for October amid ongoing voter exclusion issues.
  • India's Supreme Court reiterated that exclusion from electoral rolls does not amount to loss of citizenship, issuing notices to the Election Commission and the West Bengal government.
  • Around 34 lakh (3.4 million) appeals remain pending before appellate tribunals after the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of voter lists removed roughly 91 lakh voters in West Bengal.
  • The petition argued that deleted voters are being denied PDS rations, Annapurna scheme benefits, and caste certificates despite no final determination of their citizenship.
  • The court listed the case for August 25 and said affected individuals can approach the High Court for relief.

Court Reaffirms Citizenship Distinction

The Supreme Court on Friday made clear that removing a person's name from the electoral roll does not deprive them of their citizenship, as it heard a petition challenging the denial of welfare benefits to millions of voters excluded during the Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls in West Bengal.

A bench comprising Chief Justice of India Surya Kant, Justice Joymalya Bagchi, and Justice V. Mohana issued notices to the Election Commission of India (ECI) and the West Bengal government, seeking their responses to the petition filed by Prasenjit Bose.

"There is no confusion in law. ECI has control and superintendence over the electoral roll."

- Justice Joymalya Bagchi, Supreme Court of India

Justice Bagchi told the court that the legal position was already settled by the Supreme Court's earlier ruling on the Bihar SIR exercise: the ECI, after taking a decision on voting rights, cannot determine citizenship. The Commission has a corresponding duty to refer such matters to the Ministry for adjudication under the Citizenship Act.

Millions Left Without Benefits

The petition brought before the court the real-world consequences of the SIR exercise in West Bengal, which was conducted ahead of the state's assembly elections held in April 2026. Senior Advocate Gopal Sankaranarayanan, appearing for the petitioner, told the court that approximately 34 lakh appeals remain pending before the Special Tribunals, while only about 38,000 cases have been decided so far. Only 19 tribunals are currently functioning, and two judges have already resigned.

By April 6, around 91 lakh voters — nearly 11.9 percent of the state's electorate before the revision began — had been removed from the electoral rolls. The petition argued that those removed are now being excluded from the Public Distribution System, the Annapurna scheme, and are being denied caste certificates, even though no final decision has been made on their citizenship status.

The West Bengal government issued an order through its Food and Supplies Department directing that ration cards of individuals removed from the electoral rolls as "absent," "shifted," "duplicate," or "deceased" be marked inactive. Persons excluded after adjudication and unmapped voters who failed to establish eligibility during hearings also lost access to PDS benefits.

Passport as Proof of Citizenship

Sankaranarayanan pressed the court on the question of documentation, arguing that a valid Indian passport should be sufficient proof of citizenship.

"If you have a passport, then it should be accepted. Why need other documents?"

- Senior Advocate Gopal Sankaranarayanan

The petition also sought greater transparency in the functioning of the Special Tribunals, urging the court to direct that all tribunal orders, rules, and procedures be made publicly available on their websites. Sankaranarayanan submitted that the existing process was causing delays and discrepancies at a practical level.

Legal Background

In May 2026, the Supreme Court upheld the ECI's power to conduct the SIR while drawing a firm line between electoral roll management and citizenship adjudication. The court held that the ECI can undertake a "limited enquiry into citizenship for the purpose of satisfying itself as to eligibility for inclusion in the electoral roll," but such an enquiry "does not amount to a determination of citizenship in the strict sense."

The court directed that where the Commission is not satisfied that a person fulfils the statutory conditions for inclusion in the electoral roll on citizenship grounds, it must refer the matter to the competent authority within the Central Government. The Commission's finding, the court held, "does not operate to divest the individual of claims of citizenship."

What Comes Next

The Supreme Court has listed the case for hearing on August 25, alongside other pending matters related to the West Bengal SIR. The court also indicated that affected individuals can approach the Calcutta High Court for immediate relief. With municipal elections in West Bengal scheduled for October, the fate of millions of excluded voters — and their access to basic government services — remains unresolved.

image_caption: Chief Justice of India Surya Kant led the bench that heard arguments on welfare benefits being denied to voters deleted during the Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls in West Bengal. The court reiterated that the Election Commission cannot determine citizenship.
nri_angle: The ruling reinforces that removal from voter rolls does not affect citizenship status under the Citizenship Act, a distinction relevant to overseas Indians tracking India's evolving citizenship and documentation landscape.
